support.corpus: Middle Irish (ZCP 1, Meyer, Irish quatrains; same quatrain, second edition)

words.lemma: vid (2nd member of vasu-víd- 'goods-finding', acc. sg.)

cognate: OIr. ro-fitir ~ Ved. vid- (*weyd-, governing verb); OIr. feb ~ Ved. vásu- (*h₁wesu-, its object); OIr. ech ~ Ved. áśva- (*h₁eḱwo-) in the same verse
drift_or_renewal: Vedic víd- here is 'find, obtain' (vásu-víd- 'finding goods'), Irish ro-fitir is 'know' (the perfect, as Gk οἶδα); Irish feb is abstract 'excellence' (of horses), Vedic vásu concrete 'goods'. The horses do different jobs: Irish genitive (the excellences of horses), Vedic a simile (as steeds draw a chariot). Gk support has ἐΰ (*h₁su-), whose identity with *h₁wesu- is disputed
shared_syntax: verb of *weyd- + object noun of *h₁wesu- as the epithet of a sacred figure called on in an invocation (Irish relative clause 'who knows the excellences'; Vedic governing compound vasu-víd- in apposition to Bhaga), with *h₁eḱwo- in the same verse
context: Irish: a riding charm in a Middle Irish quatrain calling on the Cross of God and St Colmán Ela, 'who knows the excellences of horses', so that rider and horse are not thrown. AV 3.16 = RV 7.41.6: a morning invocation asking the dawns to bring Bhaga, 'the goods-finding', to the speaker as horses draw a chariot. Both are invocations of a protector described by a *weyd- + *h₁wesu- epithet, with horses in the stanza. Il. 15.679 (a trick rider 'well-skilled at riding horses', ἵπποισι κελητίζειν ἐῢ εἰδώς) shows the same horseman's-expertise collocation in Greek. Caveats: vasuvíd- is a common Vedic epithet (RV 1.18.2, 9.86.39 etc.) that has nothing to do with horses, and the Irish has only this one quatrain (no other 'fitir feba' in the Celtic layer); late Christian Irish verse. Most probably a chance meeting of common roots; reported only as a weak lead
phrase: *weyd- *h₁wesu- (+ *h₁eḱwo-): 'knows/finds the good (things)' as the epithet of a protector

note: All 203 bundles read. Pivots are almost all Middle Irish annals, saints' lives, Togail Troí and law texts; partners are mostly Greek prose. Hardly any congruent contexts. One weak claim (BC-d2afd). Leads checked and dropped: BC-cdbb5 (fáel ~ Arm. gayl 'wolf' is a word match only, contexts unrelated), BC-2c5cd grey wool (oland líath vs RV páruṣṇīm ūrṇām: contexts differ), BC-67ae2 cattle/horse ransom list vs AV gām/aśvam/pūruṣam (generic), BC-3d582 curse on corn/milk/mast (fír flathemon motif, but no cognate partner in the bundle).
